name: Merge conflict benchmarks for AI
citation: (1) Tobias Lindenbauer, Egor Bogomolov, Yaroslav Zharov (JetBrains Research; TU Munich), 'GitGoodBench: A Novel Benchmark For Evaluating Agentic Performance On Git', arXiv:2505.22583, 28 May 2025; published at REALM 2025 (1st Workshop for Research on Agent Language Models, ACL 2025, Vienna), pp. 272-288, https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.22583, https://aclanthology.org/2025.realm-1.19. (2) Qingyu Zhang, Liangcai Su, Kai Ye, Chenxiong Qian, 'CONGRA: Benchmarking Automatic Conflict Resolution', arXiv:2409.14121, 21 September 2024, https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.14121. (3) Benedikt Schesch, Michael D. Ernst (University of Washington; Schesch at Amazon, work done independently), 'Merge-Bench: Resolve Merge Conflicts with Large Language Models', arXiv:2605.25890, 25 May 2026 (also listed on Ernst's site as ICPR 2026), https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.25890. (4) Wei Zhang, Jian Yang, Jiajun Wu, Zidan Tang, Siwei Wu, 'SWE-Git-Bench: A Worktree-Level Benchmark for Real Merge Conflict Resolution', NeurIPS 2026 poster, https://neurips.cc/virtual/2026/poster/139812, code https://github.com/zwpride/SWE-Git-Bench. (5) Bowen Shen, 'Can Large Language Models Resolve Real Java Merge Conflicts? An Evaluation with a Calibrated LLM-as-Judge', arXiv:2607.27674, 30 July 2026.
evidence_tier: GitGoodBench: peer-reviewed workshop paper (REALM @ ACL 2025). SWE-Git-Bench: peer-reviewed conference poster (NeurIPS 2026). Merge-Bench: preprint, reportedly accepted at ICPR 2026 [uncertain]. ConGra and the Java LLM-as-judge study: preprints.

SWE-Git-Bench: NeurIPS abstract page only. Java judge study: arXiv abstract only. REALM venue details from search snippet.
sponsor_and_incentive: GitGoodBench is from JetBrains Research, which sells IDEs with AI assistants and Git tooling (incentive to show a gap its tools could fill). Merge-Bench authors also present their own trained model (LLMergeJ), so they benefit from showing frontier models fall short. ConGra (academic, University of Hong Kong group per affiliation [uncertain]) and the SWE-Git-Bench authors present their own benchmarks. No model vendor funded any of these as far as the opened pages show.

date_and_recency: ConGra: September 2024, models Llama3-8B, DeepSeek-V2, GLM-3-turbo, CodeLlama-7B/34B, DeepSeek-Coder (all now dated). GitGoodBench: May 2025, GPT-4o only. Merge-Bench: May 2026, frontier models of mid-2025 (Gemini 2.5 Pro, o3 Pro, Claude Opus 4, Grok 4); no GPT-5 or Claude 4.5-era models. SWE-Git-Bench: 36 LLM endpoints in a snapshot run 19-22 April 2026 (specific best model not named on the abstract page). Shen: July 2026, models not named in the abstract. As of November 2026 no benchmark found tests the latest agentic coding models (e.g. Claude Opus 4.5+, GPT-5.x) in a full agent harness on merges.
key_claims: 1) Version control work, including merges, is largely missing from mainstream coding-agent benchmarks such as SWE-bench (GitGoodBench, SWE-Git-Bench both say this). 2) GitGoodBench: GPT-4o with custom Git tools rarely reproduces the real merge exactly (13.33% solve rate on the Lite merge split, 0% on hard conflicts), although it completes most runs without error. Terminal-only access 'failed to make meaningful progress', so custom scaffolding was needed. 3) ConGra: with lenient similarity scoring, 2024 LLMs reach roughly 50-84% 'accuracy'; longer context windows did not help; general LLMs beat code LLMs; models did better on complex conflicts than simple ones; and providing surrounding conflict context hurt more often than it helped. 4) Merge-Bench (2026): on real conflict hunks capped at 20 lines per side, the best models resolve fewer than 60% correctly; Gemini 2.5 Pro leads; weaker models often leave the conflict unresolved. Results are an over-estimate for all merges because the hardest hunks were excluded. 5) SWE-Git-Bench (2026): at whole-file level the best of 36 models gets exact match on only 26.5% of files, and even all models pooled cover 41.6%. Near-identical outputs (edit similarity at least 0.99) are not safe: half of an audited 80 were labelled likely unsafe. 6) Shen (2026): on Java ConflictBench, LLMs match the developer resolution on about 55-59% of conflicts versus 36.7% for the best traditional tool (AutoMerge), mainly because tools abstain while LLMs always attempt; an LLM judge wrongly accepted most structurally broken resolutions.
headline_figures: GitGoodBench Lite (60 merge samples, GPT-4o, custom tools): merge conflict resolution 'success rate' (no system error) 76.67% (Table 2; Table 4 prints 76.76%), 'solve rate' (exact match with real resolution) 13.33%.
GitGoodBench merge solve rate by difficulty (Table 3): easy 22.58% (31 samples), medium 7.69% (13), hard 0% (16). Success rate: easy 80.64%, medium 84.62%, hard 62.5%.
GitGoodBench overall Lite solve rate across all three scenarios: 21.11% (GPT-4o). Full set 900 samples; training corpus 17,469.

ConGra accuracy (match if edit, winnowing or semantic similarity exceeds 80%): Llama3-8B Python 75.82%, Java 82.93%, C 72.45%, C++ 78.13%; DeepSeek-V2 Python 75.07%, Java 84.38%, C 54.42%, C++ 70.86%; GLM-3-turbo 57.05-64.10%; CodeLlama-7B 50.68-73.61%; CodeLlama-34B 61.47-70.82%; DeepSeek-Coder 56.49-74.52%. Dataset 44,948 conflicts from 34 projects.

Merge-Bench Java test set (806 hunks; Figure 5), code-normalised equivalent to developer resolution: Gemini 2.5 Pro 62.5% (exact text 54.7%), o3 Pro 54.3% (46.1%), Claude Opus 4 51.2% (44.4%), Grok 4 39.7% (33.4%), LLMergeJ 14B 58.9% (48.8%). Claude Opus 4 left 21.2% of hunks unresolved; Grok 4 42.4%.

Merge-Bench all-language figure (Figure 6): Gemini 2.5 Pro 47.1% exact text, 52.6% code-normalised; abstract: best models resolve 'less than 60%'. 7,938 hunks, 1,439 repos, 11 languages, hunks capped at 20 lines per side.

SWE-Git-Bench: best whole-file exact match 26.5%; oracle union across 36 models 41.6% of files; 135 conflicts / 185 conflicted files from 23 repos; conflict-block prompting +19.2 pp edit similarity, -0.1 pp exact match; 40 of 80 audited near-miss outputs (ES at least 0.99) likely unsafe. Snapshot 19-22 April 2026.

Shen 2026 (Java, ConflictBench): LLMs 55-59% match developer resolution (about 55% conservative floor) versus AutoMerge 36.7%; traditional tools abstain on 20-90%; judge 100% precision at 64.6% recall on 292 human-labelled cases.
sample_and_method: All benchmarks replay real merges from open-source repositories and compare model output with the resolution the developer actually committed; no human software engineers were studied as participants. GitGoodBench: Python, Java and Kotlin repos; GPT-4o given custom tools (view conflict, view file, view diff, resolve current conflict), conflicts resolved sequentially, scored by exact match. ConGra: 34 projects in Python, Java, C, C++; single-prompt generation per conflict; lenient similarity threshold (80%) counts as correct. Merge-Bench: single hunk, zero-shot prompt with 20 lines of context either side, not agentic; scored by exact text and code-normalised equivalence. SWE-Git-Bench: whole conflicted files from SWE-bench-family repos, 36 model endpoints, exact match plus edit similarity, plus a human audit. Shen: Java ConflictBench, generate-validate-retry solver with a calibrated LLM judge.
what_is_measured: Mechanical merge conflict resolution: given conflict markers (a hunk or a whole file), produce the resolution a developer committed. GitGoodBench also measures agentic Git use (interactive rebase, iterative committing). None measures human git fluency or whether a developer can spot a bad AI merge; they measure model ability on a narrow, convergent task.
validity_evidence: Not a hiring format; no criterion validity. As model evaluations, the metrics themselves have known validity issues: exact match understates correctness (Merge-Bench calls code matching 'a proxy for, and lower bound on, correctness'), while ConGra's 80%-similarity rule likely overstates it, and SWE-Git-Bench shows near-identical outputs can still be unsafe.
relevance_to_angle: Supports 'basic fluency still matters': no benchmark found shows models reliably resolve real merges. Best figures range from 13% exact (GPT-4o, agentic, 2025) to just under 60% (mid-2025 frontier models on small capped hunks) to 26.5% at whole-file level (April 2026), so handing even a small merge to an agent needs a human who can read the conflict and check the result. The SWE-Git-Bench audit (half of near-perfect-looking outputs likely unsafe) and Shen's finding that an LLM judge passed broken merges both support reviewing agent output rather than trusting it. It also complicates 'stop testing convergent coding' slightly: merge resolution is a convergent task where models are still weak, though the evidence argues for testing the ability to verify a merge rather than hand-merge from scratch. Caveat: the frontier models tested are a generation or more behind November 2026 agents.
limitations_stated: GitGoodBench: only GPT-4o tested; Lite set of 60 merge samples; benchmark is static ('we may need to update our benchmark with more diverse and complex scenarios'); FCC difficulty distribution may be skewed; LLM judge bias for non-merge tasks; did not test a Git MCP setup. ConGra: classifier may mislabel conflict types with advanced language features (e.g. C++ templates not captured by tree-sitter). Merge-Bench: 'The programmer merge might have been wrong'; hunk size cap 'might exclude some of the hardest merge problems ... making our results an over-estimate'; contamination likely ('almost certainly in commercial LLM training data'); training approach only evaluated on Java. Shen: an LLM judge alone should not decide structural correctness.
counter_evidence: Exact match against the developer's commit is strict: a different but correct merge counts as a failure, so true capability is higher than solve rates suggest (Merge-Bench's 'lower bound'). Shen finds LLMs beat traditional merge tools by 18-22 points, mostly by always attempting a resolution, so LLMs are already more useful than existing automation. ConGra's lenient scoring shows 2024 models getting 75-84% on some languages. None of the benchmarks tests a current agent (Claude Code, Codex and similar) with full repository access, the ability to run tests and build, and the latest models; such a setup could do much better, especially on small merges. GitGoodBench's 76.67% 'success rate' is often misread as accuracy; it only means no error occurred.
